Liver function tests are a group of blood tests that assess hepatocellular injury, cholestasis, and the synthetic and excretory capacity of the liver. Reference ranges vary between laboratories.

| Group | Test | Approximate normal value | Significance |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Excretory function** | Total serum bilirubin | 0.3–1.2 mg/dL (5–21 µmol/L) | Raised in haemolysis, hepatocellular disease, obstruction |
| | Conjugated (direct) bilirubin | 0–0.3 mg/dL | Raised in hepatocellular disease and obstruction |
| **Hepatocellular injury** | Alanine aminotransferase (ALT/SGPT) | about 7–55 U/L | Markedly raised in hepatitis |
| | Aspartate aminotransferase (AST/SGOT) | about 8–48 U/L | Raised in hepatitis; AST:ALT ratio of 2:1 or more in alcohol-associated disease |
| **Cholestasis** | Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) | about 40–130 U/L | Markedly raised in obstruction and infiltrative disease |
| | Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) | about 8–60 U/L | Raised in cholestasis and alcohol use; confirms hepatic origin of ALP |
| **Synthetic function** | Serum albumin | 3.5–5.0 g/dL | Reduced in chronic liver disease |
| | Total protein; globulin | 6.0–8.3 g/dL; 2.0–3.5 g/dL | Globulins raised in chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis |
| | Prothrombin time (INR) | 11–13.5 seconds (INR 0.8–1.2) | Prolonged in hepatocellular failure and vitamin K deficiency |

Additional tests include serum ammonia, 5′-nucleotidase, serum cholesterol, bile acids, and α-fetoprotein. Because the liver has a large reserve, tests can remain normal until 80% to 90% of functional capacity is lost, and abnormalities should be interpreted as a pattern (hepatocellular, cholestatic, or mixed) in the clinical context.


## Name synthetic liver function tests.

The synthetic liver function tests, which assess the capacity of the liver to synthesise proteins, are:

1. **Serum albumin** (half-life about 20 days)
2. **Prothrombin time and INR**, reflecting synthesis of clotting factors II (prothrombin), V, VII, IX, and X (factor VII has the shortest half-life)
3. Serum fibrinogen and other clotting factors
4. Serum pseudocholinesterase and serum cholesterol (to a lesser degree)


## Name two causes of raised prothrombin time.

1. **Hepatocellular disease or liver failure** (acute liver failure, cirrhosis), because the hepatocytes synthesise the clotting factors II, V, VII, IX, X, XI, and XII and fibrinogen; the prolongation is not corrected by parenteral vitamin K.
2. **Vitamin K deficiency**, as in obstructive jaundice (bile salt deficiency causes malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins) or malabsorption syndromes; the prolongation is corrected by parenteral vitamin K.

Other causes: warfarin therapy and disseminated intravascular coagulation.


## Why is prothrombin time more specific than total protein estimation?

Prothrombin time is a more specific and sensitive indicator of hepatic synthetic function than total protein for the following reasons:

1. The clotting factors measured by the prothrombin time (especially factor VII, with a half-life of about 4 to 6 hours) have a very short half-life, so the test reflects the current synthetic capacity of the liver and falls within hours to days of acute hepatocellular damage, whereas albumin has a half-life of about 20 days and so changes slowly.
2. Total protein is the sum of albumin and globulins. In chronic liver disease albumin falls but globulins rise (polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia due to impaired clearance of antigens by the Kupffer cells and shunting), so the total protein may remain normal and mask the hepatic dysfunction.
3. Total protein is also influenced by nutrition, protein-losing states (nephrotic syndrome, protein-losing enteropathy), hydration, and chronic inflammation or myeloma, which are not related to liver function.
4. The clotting factors are synthesised almost exclusively by the liver, and a prolonged prothrombin time that is not corrected by vitamin K indicates a severe hepatocellular defect and has prognostic value (it is part of the MELD and Child–Pugh scores).


## Name common pathological conditions of hepatomegaly.

Hepatomegaly may result from the following groups of conditions.

| Mechanism | Examples |
|---|---|
| Inflammation and infection | Acute viral hepatitis, alcohol-associated hepatitis, liver abscess (pyogenic, amoebic), malaria, kala-azar, typhoid, hydatid cyst, schistosomiasis |
| Fatty infiltration | Alcohol-associated fatty liver, metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease, diabetes, obesity |
| Congestion | Right-sided or congestive heart failure, constrictive pericarditis, Budd–Chiari syndrome |
| Biliary obstruction | Extrahepatic obstruction (stones, tumour) and cholangitis |
| Cirrhosis | Early cirrhosis (enlarged, nodular liver; later shrunken) |
| Neoplasms | Hepatocellular carcinoma and metastatic carcinoma (massive nodular hepatomegaly), haemangioma |
| Infiltrative and storage disorders | Amyloidosis, haemochromatosis, Wilson disease, glycogen storage disease, Gaucher disease, sarcoidosis |
| Haematological | Leukaemias, lymphomas, myeloproliferative disorders, thalassaemia, sickle cell disease with extramedullary haematopoiesis |

## Name the hepatotropic viruses.

The hepatotropic viruses are **hepatitis A virus (HAV)**, **hepatitis B virus (HBV)**, **hepatitis C virus (HCV)**, **hepatitis D virus (HDV, the delta agent)**, and **hepatitis E virus (HEV)**. HAV and HEV are transmitted by the fecal–oral route and cause only acute disease (HEV may be chronic in the immunocompromised), while HBV, HCV, and HDV are transmitted parenterally and can cause chronic hepatitis. Nonhepatotropic viruses such as Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, adenovirus, and yellow fever virus may also involve the liver.


## Discuss the clinical outcomes of hepatitis B virus infection.

The outcome of HBV infection depends on the age at exposure, the immune competence of the host, and co-infection with other agents. Cytotoxic CD8⁺ T cells directed against infected hepatocytes cause most of the injury, and a strong virus-specific CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T-cell response is associated with resolution.

**Acute infection.** After an incubation period of 4 to 26 weeks, acute infection is mild or subclinical in about two-thirds of adults and may present with anorexia, fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain, with a preicteric, icteric, and convalescent phase. Most patients clear the virus, with disappearance of HBsAg within about 12 weeks (up to 24), and appearance of anti-HBs. Immune-complex phenomena such as glomerulonephritis and polyarteritis nodosa may occur.

**Acute liver failure.** Occurs in about 0.1% to 0.5% of acutely infected individuals, within 4 to 8 weeks, with massive hepatic necrosis, encephalopathy, and coagulopathy; HDV co-infection increases the risk.

**Chronic hepatitis.** Develops in 5% to 10% of adults, but in about 90% of infants infected at birth, with persistence of HBsAg and HBV DNA. Persistent HBeAg indicates continued replication and probable progression. Chronic hepatitis is defined as symptomatic, biochemical, or serologic evidence of continuing or relapsing disease for more than 6 months, or the presence of fibrosis. Progression to cirrhosis occurs over years (average about 8), with portal hypertension, liver failure, and decompensation.

**Carrier state.** An individual who harbors the virus but has no symptoms; the "healthy carrier" has HBsAg and anti-HBe, normal aminotransferases, low HBV DNA, and no significant liver damage.

**Hepatocellular carcinoma.** Chronic HBV infection, especially acquired perinatally, carries a high risk of HCC, through the integration of viral DNA, the transcriptional activation by HBx, and chronic injury and regeneration; it may arise in noncirrhotic liver.

**HDV.** Co-infection causes acute hepatitis that is usually self-limited, while superinfection of a chronic carrier causes severe acute hepatitis or exacerbation, with chronic HDV in more than 80%, and accelerates progression to cirrhosis and HCC.

Antiviral therapy (interferon, entecavir, tenofovir) slows progression, and vaccination prevents infection (protective anti-HBs in 95%).


## Mention the microscopic features of liver in acute and chronic viral hepatitis.

The microscopic changes in acute and chronic viral hepatitis due to the hepatotropic viruses are largely similar and overlap with those of autoimmune hepatitis, drug reactions, and Wilson disease.

**Acute viral hepatitis.**

1. Lobular and portal inflammation, predominantly lymphocytes, with variable plasma cells and eosinophils, and activation of Kupffer cells.
2. Hepatocyte injury: ballooning degeneration (swelling with clear cytoplasm) and necrosis or apoptosis; apoptotic cells appear as shrunken, eosinophilic acidophil (Councilman) bodies; pigmented macrophages scavenge dead cell debris.
3. In severe cases, confluent necrosis of groups of cells that may become bridging necrosis (connecting portal tracts to central veins or portal tracts to each other) and, with massive necrosis, panlobular necrosis and collapse of the reticulin framework.
4. Cholestasis (bile plugs) may be present, and regeneration (binucleate hepatocytes, thickened plates) is evident.

**Chronic viral hepatitis.**

1. The defining feature is portal lymphocytic or lymphoplasmacytic inflammation with fibrosis; inflammatory cells cross the limiting plate and injure periportal hepatocytes (interface hepatitis, formerly piecemeal necrosis), with a variable degree of lobular inflammation.
2. Fibrosis progresses from portal and periportal fibrosis to portoportal bridging fibrosis and finally cirrhosis.
3. **Chronic hepatitis B**: "ground-glass" hepatocytes, with cytoplasm filled with HBsAg in swollen endoplasmic reticulum (confirmed by immunostaining for HBsAg and HBcAg).
4. **Chronic hepatitis C**: prominent portal lymphoid aggregates or follicles, steatosis (marked with genotype 3), and focal bile duct injury.
5. Biopsy is used to grade the inflammatory activity and stage the fibrosis.


## What alterations occur in liver function tests in acute viral hepatitis / chronic liver disease?

**Acute viral hepatitis.**

- **Serum aminotransferases (ALT and AST)** are markedly raised (often several hundred to thousands of units per litre), and the rise precedes the jaundice; ALT is usually higher than AST. A fall in transaminases with worsening jaundice and coagulopathy is a sign of massive necrosis.
- **Serum bilirubin** is raised (mixed conjugated and unconjugated), with bilirubinuria preceding the clinical jaundice; urinary urobilinogen is increased early.
- **Alkaline phosphatase** is normal or only mildly raised (cholestatic features in some cases of hepatitis A).
- **Prothrombin time** is prolonged in severe disease; this signifies a poor prognosis.
- Serum albumin is usually normal because of its long half-life.

**Chronic liver disease (chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis).**

- Aminotransferases are mildly to moderately raised and fluctuate, and may be normal in cirrhosis.
- **Serum albumin is reduced** (hypoalbuminaemia), while globulins are raised (hypergammaglobulinaemia), reversing the albumin:globulin ratio.
- **Prothrombin time is prolonged**, and not corrected by vitamin K.
- Serum bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase are variably raised, and ammonia may be raised.
- Haematologic changes of hypersplenism: thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and anaemia.
- In advanced disease, hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, and raised creatinine (hepatorenal syndrome).


## A 30y male with recent blood transfusion has jaundice, weakness. What are the possible fates/outcomes of such a case?

A jaundiced young adult with a recent history of blood transfusion most probably has **acute viral hepatitis acquired parenterally, due to hepatitis B or hepatitis C**. The possible outcomes are:

1. **Complete recovery** with clearance of the virus and immunity (usual in acute HBV infection of adults; HBsAg disappears and anti-HBs appears).
2. **Acute liver failure** (fulminant hepatitis) from massive hepatic necrosis, with encephalopathy and coagulopathy; rare (0.1% to 0.5% in HBV), and fatal without transplantation.
3. **Chronic hepatitis**, in 5% to 10% of adults with HBV and in more than 80% of those with HCV (acute HCV is often asymptomatic).
4. **Cirrhosis**, with portal hypertension, ascites, varices, encephalopathy, and liver failure, in about 20% of chronic HCV patients over 20 to 30 years.
5. **Hepatocellular carcinoma** in chronic HBV or HCV, especially with cirrhosis.
6. **Asymptomatic carrier state** in HBV, a reservoir of infection.
7. **Extrahepatic immune-complex disease** (glomerulonephritis, vasculitis, cryoglobulinaemia).


## Same (with anorexia, high SGPT): what is the provisional diagnosis?

The provisional diagnosis is **acute viral hepatitis**, most likely hepatitis B (or C) acquired through the blood transfusion. The prodromal anorexia, malaise, and jaundice, with a markedly raised serum alanine aminotransferase (SGPT), indicate hepatocellular injury. It is confirmed by serology (HBsAg and anti-HBc IgM; anti-HCV and HCV RNA; anti-HAV IgM and anti-HEV IgM to exclude other viruses), liver function tests, and prothrombin time; a liver biopsy is not required in acute disease.

## Give an outline of the spectrum of liver diseases associated with alcohol abuse.

Alcohol-associated liver disease has three distinctive, overlapping forms: hepatic steatosis, alcoholic (alcohol-associated) steatohepatitis, and fibrosis leading to cirrhosis. Short-term ingestion of about 80 g of alcohol per day produces mild reversible steatosis, the risk of severe injury becomes significant at 80 g or more per day, and 160 g or more daily for 10 to 20 years is frequently associated with severe injury; only 10% to 15% of persons with alcohol use disorder develop cirrhosis. Women are more susceptible, and genetic factors, iron overload, and HBV or HCV infection modify the risk. The injury begins in the centrilobular (zone 3) region.

| Stage | Pathology | Clinical features |
|---|---|---|
| **Alcoholic fatty liver (steatosis)** | Macrovesicular steatosis (small droplets coalescing to large), the liver is large (up to 4 to 6 kg), soft, yellow, and greasy; reversible with abstinence | Often asymptomatic; hepatomegaly; mild elevation of bilirubin and ALP |
| **Alcoholic hepatitis (steatohepatitis)** | Ballooned hepatocytes with Mallory–Denk hyaline (keratin 8 and 18), neutrophilic infiltrate (satellitosis), lobular inflammation, spotty necrosis, steatosis, pericellular ("chicken-wire") perivenular fibrosis | Acute illness after a heavy bout: malaise, anorexia, fever, tender hepatomegaly, jaundice, neutrophilic leukocytosis; AST:ALT 2:1 or greater; mortality 10% to 20% per episode |
| **Alcoholic cirrhosis** | Micronodular (Laennec) cirrhosis, later mixed; progressive fibrosis with vascular derangement | Features of portal hypertension and liver failure; may be silent; complicated by variceal bleeding, hepatic coma, hepatorenal syndrome, infection, and hepatocellular carcinoma (1% to 6% per year) |

**Pathogenesis.** Alcohol is metabolised by alcohol dehydrogenase to acetaldehyde (generating NADH, which promotes lipogenesis and suppresses fatty acid oxidation), and by CYP2E1, which generates reactive oxygen species. Acetaldehyde forms protein adducts and induces lipid peroxidation. Gut-derived endotoxin activates Kupffer cells through TLR4, with release of cytokines, and stellate cell activation causes fibrosis.

**Prognosis.** The 5-year survival approaches 90% in abstainers without jaundice, ascites, or haematemesis but falls to 50% to 60% in those who continue to drink; the death is due to hepatic coma, gastrointestinal haemorrhage, infection, hepatorenal syndrome, or hepatocellular carcinoma.

## Define cirrhosis of liver.

Cirrhosis is a diffuse process involving the entire liver, characterised by the conversion of the normal lobular architecture into parenchymal nodules (usually regenerative) surrounded by dense bands of fibrous tissue, with a variable degree of vascular, often portosystemic, shunting. It is the end stage of chronic liver injury of many causes; the liver surface becomes bumpy with depressed scars and bulging nodules. The key features are the diffuse nature, the bridging fibrosis, the nodule formation, and the disruption of the vascular architecture, which causes portal hypertension and impairs hepatocellular function.


## Name the etiology of cirrhosis.

The aetiology of cirrhosis includes:

1. Chronic viral hepatitis (B, B with D, and C)
2. Alcohol-associated liver disease
3. Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH)
4. Chronic biliary disease: primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, chronic biliary obstruction, biliary atresia
5. Autoimmune hepatitis
6. Inherited metabolic disease: haemochromatosis, Wilson disease, α₁-antitrypsin deficiency
7. Chronic hepatic venous congestion: Budd–Chiari syndrome, right-sided heart failure
8. Drugs and toxins
9. Chronic schistosomiasis
10. Cryptogenic (unknown cause)


## Write the etiopathogenesis of cirrhosis.

Cirrhosis represents the common end point of repeated, prolonged hepatic injury, chronic inflammation, and the repair process, regardless of the underlying cause.

**Aetiology.** The major causes are chronic viral hepatitis B and C, alcohol-associated liver disease, MASH, chronic biliary disease, autoimmune hepatitis, inherited metabolic diseases (haemochromatosis, Wilson disease, α₁-antitrypsin deficiency), venous outflow obstruction, and drugs.

**Pathogenesis.**

1. **Persistent hepatocellular injury and inflammation**: Hepatocyte death by necrosis or apoptosis, with an inflammatory response by Kupffer cells and lymphocytes, releases cytokines and growth factors (TGF-β, PDGF, TNF, IL-1) and reactive oxygen species.
2. **Activation of hepatic stellate cells**: The stellate cells in the space of Disse, which normally store vitamin A, are activated by these mediators and by injury to the sinusoidal endothelium; they transform into myofibroblast-like cells that proliferate and synthesise large amounts of collagen types I and III and other matrix proteins. Portal fibroblasts and bone marrow–derived cells contribute.
3. **Progressive fibrosis**: The fibrosis begins in portal tracts or around the central veins (depending on the disease), progresses to bridging septa that link portal tracts to each other or to central veins, and finally subdivides the parenchyma. Capillarisation of the sinusoids (deposition of matrix in the space of Disse and loss of endothelial fenestrae) impairs exchange between blood and hepatocytes.
4. **Regeneration and nodule formation**: Surviving hepatocytes regenerate as nodules, isolated from their blood supply by fibrous septa, with a ductular reaction and stem-cell activation; the nodular architecture compresses the vessels.
5. **Vascular derangement**: Distortion and obliteration of the hepatic and portal vessels, with arterioportal anastomoses and shunts, increases the resistance to portal flow (portal hypertension) and decreases the perfusion of hepatocytes (hepatic failure).
6. **Failure of matrix degradation**: The balance between matrix metalloproteinases and their tissue inhibitors (TIMPs) shifts toward matrix accumulation. Early fibrosis may regress when the cause is removed, but established cirrhosis with vascular remodeling rarely reverses completely.


## What are the complications of cirrhosis?

About 40% of patients are asymptomatic until late. The complications result from portal hypertension and hepatocellular failure.

**Portal hypertension and its consequences.**

1. **Ascites**, which may be complicated by spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and hydrothorax.
2. **Portosystemic shunts**: oesophagogastric varices (haemorrhage), haemorrhoids, caput medusae, and retroperitoneal collaterals.
3. **Congestive splenomegaly** with hypersplenism (thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, anaemia).

**Hepatic failure.**

4. **Hepatic encephalopathy** and coma.
5. **Coagulopathy** (bruising, bleeding, DIC).
6. **Jaundice** and cholestasis with pruritus.
7. **Hepatorenal syndrome**.
8. **Hyperoestrogenism**: palmar erythema, spider angiomas, gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy, and hypogonadism.
9. **Hypoalbuminaemia and oedema**; malnutrition and muscle wasting.
10. **Pulmonary complications**: hepatopulmonary syndrome and portopulmonary hypertension.
11. **Infections** (impaired Kupffer cell function and gut barrier loss).

**Neoplastic.**

12. **Hepatocellular carcinoma**, which develops in many cirrhotic livers (1% to 6% annually in alcohol-associated cirrhosis).

**Others.** Portal vein thrombosis and acute-on-chronic liver failure.


## How is ascites formed in cirrhosis of liver?

Ascites is the accumulation of excess fluid (usually serous, with less than 3 g/dL protein, and a serum-to-ascites albumin gradient of 1.1 g/dL or more) in the peritoneal cavity; cirrhosis causes 85% of cases, and it becomes clinically detectable when at least 500 mL has accumulated. Its pathogenesis is multifactorial:

1. **Sinusoidal (portal) hypertension.** Raised hydrostatic pressure in the portal venous system and hepatic sinusoids increases the filtration of fluid into the space of Disse; the excess hepatic lymph (hepatic lymph flow can increase up to 20-fold) exceeds the capacity of the lymphatics and weeps from the surface of the liver into the peritoneal cavity. Increased splanchnic capillary pressure also adds to the transudation.
2. **Hypoalbuminaemia.** Reduced hepatic synthesis of albumin lowers the plasma oncotic pressure, so fluid is retained in the interstitium and peritoneal cavity.
3. **Splanchnic arterial vasodilation (nitric oxide–mediated) and hyperdynamic circulation.** Systemic arterial underfilling decreases the effective circulating volume and activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, sympathetic nervous system, and antidiuretic hormone, causing renal retention of sodium and water, which maintains and amplifies the ascites. Reduced hepatic inactivation of aldosterone contributes.
4. **Increased hepatic and splanchnic lymph production** and renal sodium retention.

The fluid may become infected (spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, with neutrophils in the fluid), and long-standing ascites may cause hydrothorax (usually right-sided) by passage through diaphragmatic lymphatics.


## Write the mechanism of cirrhotic death.

Death in cirrhosis results from the progressive loss of hepatocellular function and from the complications of portal hypertension. The common proximate causes are:

1. **Hepatic failure with hepatic encephalopathy and coma**: failure of the liver to detoxify ammonia and other gut-derived toxins (and shunting of portal blood around the liver) leads to cerebral dysfunction and oedema, often precipitated by gastrointestinal bleeding, infection, electrolyte disturbance, or sedatives.
2. **Massive haemorrhage from oesophagogastric varices**: about 40% of patients with advanced cirrhosis develop varices, and each bleeding episode carries a mortality of 15% to 30%; the blood load in the gut also precipitates encephalopathy.
3. **Infections**: sepsis, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and pneumonia, caused by impaired Kupffer cell function, gut mucosal barrier damage, and immune dysfunction.
4. **Hepatorenal syndrome**: renal failure due to splanchnic vasodilation, activation of the renin–angiotensin axis, and renal vasoconstriction.
5. **Hepatocellular carcinoma**, developing in the cirrhotic liver.
6. **Coagulopathy and multiorgan failure**, with acute-on-chronic liver failure precipitated by sepsis, drugs, or portal vein thrombosis.


## A male has jaundice, gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy/abdominal distension, ascites. What is the likely diagnosis?

The likely diagnosis is **cirrhosis of the liver (decompensated), with portal hypertension**, most commonly alcohol-associated or post-viral. Jaundice reflects hepatocellular failure, gynaecomastia and testicular atrophy result from hyperoestrogenaemia and hypogonadism due to impaired hepatic oestrogen metabolism, and the abdominal distension with ascites results from portal hypertension, hypoalbuminaemia, and renal salt and water retention. Palmar erythema, spider angiomas, caput medusae, splenomegaly, and hepatic encephalopathy may coexist. The diagnosis is established by liver function tests, ultrasonography, endoscopy, ascitic fluid analysis, and, where appropriate, liver biopsy.


## Same (40y): name the liver function tests expected to be altered.

In cirrhosis the following liver function tests are expected to be altered:

1. **Serum bilirubin** is raised (conjugated and unconjugated).
2. **Aminotransferases (AST, ALT)** are mildly to moderately raised (AST greater than ALT in alcohol-associated disease), and may be normal in advanced disease.
3. **Alkaline phosphatase and GGT** are variably raised.
4. **Serum albumin** is reduced and **globulins** are raised, so the albumin:globulin ratio is reversed.
5. **Prothrombin time (INR)** is prolonged and is not corrected by vitamin K.
6. Serum ammonia may be raised, and cholesterol low in advanced disease.


## What is hepatic encephalopathy?

Hepatic encephalopathy is a spectrum of potentially reversible neuropsychiatric disturbances of consciousness and behaviour, ranging from subtle changes in personality, sleep reversal, and confusion, through stupor, to deep coma and death, that complicates acute or chronic liver failure and portosystemic shunting.

**Pathogenesis.** It is believed to be caused by elevated blood ammonia, which correlates with impaired neuronal function and cerebral oedema. The principal source of ammonia is the gastrointestinal tract, where it is produced by gut bacteria and by enterocytes during glutamine metabolism. Normally the ammonia travels in the portal vein to the liver, where it is converted to urea by the urea cycle; in severe liver disease, or when the portal blood bypasses the liver through shunts, this detoxification fails. In the brain, astrocytes metabolise ammonia to glutamine, which acts as an osmolyte and causes astrocyte swelling and cerebral oedema; ammonia also directly affects neurons and neurotransmission. Other contributors are false neurotransmitters, increased GABAergic tone, inflammation, and infection.

**Clinical features.** Behavioural abnormalities, altered sleep rhythm, confusion, drowsiness, stupor, and coma; fluctuating neurological signs including rigidity and hyperreflexia; **asterixis** (flapping tremor: nonrhythmic rapid extension–flexion of the head and extremities, best seen with the arms outstretched and wrists dorsiflexed); fetor hepaticus; raised blood ammonia; and slowing of the electroencephalogram.

**Precipitating factors.** Gastrointestinal haemorrhage, infection, constipation, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalaemia, alkalosis), a high-protein load, sedatives, diuretics, and renal failure.

**Management.** Correction of precipitating factors, lactulose and rifaximin to reduce ammonia production and absorption, and protein-appropriate nutrition; liver transplantation in refractory cases.

## Enumerate the important causes of ascites.

The important causes of ascites are:

1. **Cirrhosis of the liver** (commonest, 85% of cases), and other causes of portal hypertension: portal vein thrombosis, Budd–Chiari syndrome, and schistosomiasis.
2. **Cardiac**: congestive cardiac failure and constrictive pericarditis.
3. **Renal**: nephrotic syndrome and chronic kidney disease.
4. **Hypoalbuminaemia** from malnutrition and protein-losing enteropathy.
5. **Peritoneal disease**: tuberculous peritonitis, peritoneal carcinomatosis, and other causes of peritonitis.
6. **Malignancy**: metastatic disease of the liver and peritoneum, and ovarian tumours (Meigs syndrome).
7. **Pancreatic disease** (pancreatic ascites) and lymphatic obstruction (chylous ascites).
8. Myxoedema.

## Write down the etiology of hepatocellular carcinoma.

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) accounts for about 5.4% of all cancers worldwide. Most cases (more than 85%) occur in Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, where chronic hepatitis B is common, and about 80% to 85% arise in a cirrhotic liver, although 15% to 20% arise in noncirrhotic liver. The unifying mechanism is chronic liver injury, with inflammation and repeated hepatocyte regeneration, leading to the acquisition of driver mutations. The aetiological factors are:

1. **Chronic hepatitis B virus infection**, the leading cause worldwide, especially when acquired perinatally; it acts through chronic inflammation and regeneration, integration of viral DNA, and the HBx protein, and may cause HCC without cirrhosis.
2. **Chronic hepatitis C virus infection**, usually through cirrhosis (about one-third of HCC in the United States).
3. **Alcohol-associated liver disease** and cirrhosis from any cause.
4. **Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease/steatohepatitis**, with obesity and diabetes, increasing in Western countries, which may cause HCC even without cirrhosis.
5. **Aflatoxin B₁**, a mycotoxin produced by Aspergillus contaminating stored grain and groundnuts, which causes TP53 mutation (codon 249) and acts synergistically with hepatitis B.
6. **Inherited metabolic diseases**: hereditary haemochromatosis, α₁-antitrypsin deficiency, tyrosinaemia, and, less often, Wilson disease and chronic biliary diseases.
7. **Hepatocellular adenoma** (particularly with β-catenin mutation) and anabolic androgenic steroid use.
8. Others: tobacco smoking, and male sex (up to 8:1 in high-incidence areas).

Common driver mutations are activating mutations of CTNNB1 (β-catenin, about 40%), TERT promoter mutations (50% to 60%), and inactivating TP53 mutations (up to 60%); the fibrolamellar variant carries the DNAJB1::PRKACA fusion.


## A 59y male with HBV history has hepatomegaly, SOL in right lobe on USG. How will you proceed to diagnose?

A 59-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B and a space-occupying lesion in the right lobe of the liver must be assumed to have **hepatocellular carcinoma** until proven otherwise (the other possibilities being a regenerative or dysplastic nodule, haemangioma, abscess, cholangiocarcinoma, and metastasis). The diagnosis proceeds as follows.

1. **History and examination**: duration of HBV infection, alcohol, constitutional symptoms (weight loss, pain), and signs of chronic liver disease (jaundice, ascites, splenomegaly, spider angiomas); a nodular hard liver.
2. **Serum α-fetoprotein (AFP)**: a markedly raised level (above 400 ng/mL) supports HCC, although it is not sensitive for early tumours and is not raised in the fibrolamellar variant. Des-γ-carboxy prothrombin may be added.
3. **Multiphase (triphasic) contrast-enhanced CT or MRI**: the characteristic pattern in a cirrhotic liver is arterial-phase hyperenhancement with rapid venous-phase washout, which is diagnostic in an at-risk patient without biopsy; it also shows the number and size of the lesions, vascular invasion (portal vein thrombosis), and extrahepatic spread.
4. **Image-guided percutaneous needle biopsy (or fine needle aspiration cytology)** if imaging is indeterminate, with histology and immunostaining (glypican-3, HepPar-1, arginase-1); the risk is tumour seeding along the needle track and bleeding.
5. **Assessment of the underlying liver disease and function**: liver function tests, prothrombin time, albumin, bilirubin (Child–Pugh score), HBV DNA, HBsAg, anti-HCV, upper endoscopy for varices, and platelet count.
6. **Staging**: chest CT for lung metastases, bone scan if indicated, and staging systems such as BCLC to plan treatment (resection, transplantation, ablation, chemoembolisation, or systemic therapy).


## Same: what are your expected findings?

**Clinical.** Abdominal pain or discomfort, weight loss, fatigue, anorexia, and a firm, nodular, tender hepatomegaly, sometimes with a bruit over the liver; features of underlying chronic liver disease (jaundice, ascites, splenomegaly, collaterals); sudden deterioration of a known cirrhosis may signal the tumour. Complications are portal vein invasion, variceal bleeding, rupture with haemoperitoneum, and paraneoplastic syndromes (erythrocytosis, hypoglycaemia, hypercalcaemia).

**Laboratory.** Raised serum α-fetoprotein (a frequent finding in advanced disease), raised alkaline phosphatase and GGT, abnormal liver function tests reflecting the cirrhosis, positive HBsAg, and HBV DNA.

**Imaging.** Ultrasonography shows a focal mass, usually hypoechoic or heterogeneous, and the multiphase CT or MRI shows arterial enhancement with early washout in the venous phase; there may be tumour thrombus in the portal or hepatic veins.

**Gross.** A single mass, multiple discrete nodules, or a diffusely infiltrative tumour, pale yellow if fatty, green if cholestatic, often in a cirrhotic liver; tumours larger than 2 cm are more likely to show vascular invasion and intrahepatic metastases, and invasion of veins may extend into the portal vein, inferior vena cava, and right heart.

**Microscopic.** Well and moderately differentiated tumours resemble normal hepatocytes, growing as thick trabeculae (more than 3 cells thick), pseudoglandular structures with bile plugs, or sheets; the poorly differentiated tumours show marked atypia. Precursors are dysplastic nodules in a cirrhotic liver (large and small cell change). The fibrolamellar variant (adolescents and young adults, normal AFP) shows large polygonal oncocytic cells, prominent nucleoli, and lamellar collagen bundles.

**Spread.** Haematogenous metastasis (lung, bone) late; lymph node spread in fewer than 5%. The 5-year survival is about 30% for localised disease and 5% to 10% with extrahepatic spread.

## What are the factors that favour stone formation within gallbladder?

**Cholesterol stones.** Four conditions contribute to the formation of cholesterol stones:

1. **Supersaturation of bile with cholesterol**: cholesterol is rendered soluble by micelles formed with bile salts and lecithin; when cholesterol secretion exceeds the solubilising capacity (hypersecretion of cholesterol, or reduced bile salt pool), crystals can nucleate. This is favoured by oestrogen (female sex, pregnancy, oral contraceptives, which increase hepatic cholesterol uptake and HMG-CoA reductase activity), obesity, rapid weight loss, age, and ileal disease or resection with loss of bile salts.
2. **Gallbladder hypomotility (stasis)**: neurogenic or hormonal, as in pregnancy, prolonged fasting, parenteral nutrition, and rapid weight loss.
3. **Accelerated cholesterol crystal nucleation** by pronucleating factors (mucin glycoproteins, calcium).
4. **Hypersecretion of mucus** in the gallbladder, which traps the nucleated crystals and promotes their aggregation into stones.

**Pigment stones.** Elevated unconjugated bilirubin in bile, due to chronic haemolysis, bacterial and parasitic infection of the biliary tree (β-glucuronidase release by E. coli, Ascaris, liver flukes), ileal dysfunction, and cirrhosis, with biliary stasis.

**Other factors**: genetic variants of biliary lipid transporters (ABCG8), diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidaemia.


## Classify glomerular disease.

Glomerular diseases can be classified in three complementary ways: by origin, by the clinical syndrome they produce, and by the morphological pattern of injury.

**1. Classification by origin**

Primary glomerular diseases are those in which the kidney is the only or predominant organ involved. Some have a prominent inflammatory (proliferative) component and are therefore called glomerulonephritis; others, such as minimal change disease and membranous nephropathy, lack a cellular inflammatory component and are more correctly termed glomerulopathies.

- Acute proliferative (postinfectious, e.g., poststreptococcal) glomerulonephritis
- Rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis — anti-GBM antibody–mediated, immune complex–mediated, or pauci-immune (ANCA-associated)
- Membranous nephropathy
- Minimal change disease
- Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)
- Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (immune complex–mediated) and C3 glomerulopathies (dense deposit disease and C3 glomerulonephritis)
- IgA nephropathy
- Fibrillary glomerulonephritis
- Hereditary glomerular diseases — Alport syndrome and thin basement membrane nephropathy; congenital nephrotic syndrome due to nephrin or podocin mutations

Secondary glomerular diseases arise as one manifestation of a systemic disorder: systemic lupus erythematosus (lupus nephritis), diabetes mellitus (diabetic nephropathy), amyloidosis, Goodpasture syndrome, IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura), granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis, infective endocarditis, hepatitis B and C, HIV, malaria, syphilis and schistosomiasis, thrombotic microangiopathies (HUS/TTP), monoclonal immunoglobulin (myeloma-related) deposition disease, Fabry disease, and drug-induced lesions. Both the clinical manifestations and the histological changes of primary and secondary forms may be similar, which is why a systemic cause must always be sought.

**2. Classification by clinical syndrome**

| Syndrome | Principal features | Typical diseases |
|---|---|---|
| Nephritic syndrome | Haematuria, azotaemia, oliguria, mild–moderate proteinuria, hypertension | Acute postinfectious GN, IgA nephropathy, lupus nephritis |
| Rapidly progressive GN | Nephritic picture with rapid loss of GFR over days to weeks | Crescentic GN (anti-GBM, immune complex, ANCA) |
| Nephrotic syndrome | Proteinuria >3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, hyperlipidaemia, lipiduria | Minimal change disease, membranous nephropathy, FSGS, diabetic nephropathy |
| Isolated urinary abnormalities | Asymptomatic haematuria and/or subnephrotic proteinuria | IgA nephropathy, Alport syndrome, thin basement membrane disease |
| Chronic kidney disease | Azotaemia progressing to uraemia over months to years | End stage of any of the above |

**3. Classification by morphology**

The glomerular lesion is described as diffuse (involving all or most glomeruli) or focal (involving only some); global (the whole tuft affected) or segmental (only part of the tuft). It is further described as proliferative (endocapillary — endothelial, mesangial and leukocytic hypercellularity; or extracapillary — crescent formation) or nonproliferative (membranous change, minimal change). Membranoproliferative lesions combine capillary wall thickening with proliferation, and sclerosing lesions (FSGS, diabetic glomerulosclerosis) are characterised by obliteration of capillary lumens by matrix.


## Name the primary glomerular diseases.

The primary glomerular diseases are:

1. Acute proliferative (postinfectious) glomerulonephritis
2. Rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis
3. Membranous nephropathy
4. Minimal change disease
5. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
6. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (immune complex–mediated)
7. C3 glomerulopathy — dense deposit disease and C3 glomerulonephritis
8. IgA nephropathy
9. Fibrillary glomerulonephritis

Hereditary disorders of the glomerulus, notably Alport syndrome and thin basement membrane nephropathy, are usually considered alongside these as glomerular diseases causing isolated haematuria.


## What is nephrotic syndrome?

Nephrotic syndrome is a clinical complex caused by a derangement of the glomerular capillary wall that makes it abnormally permeable to plasma proteins. It is defined by four features: (1) massive proteinuria, with loss of 3.5 g or more of protein in the urine per day (a lesser threshold, adjusted for body size, applies in children); (2) hypoalbuminaemia, with plasma albumin below 3 g/dL; (3) generalised oedema; and (4) hyperlipidaemia with lipiduria.

These components are logically related. The glomerular filtration barrier, composed of fenestrated endothelium, glomerular basement membrane and the podocyte slit diaphragm, normally restricts protein passage by size and charge. When structural or physicochemical injury to this barrier increases its permeability, albumin and other proteins escape into the urine. Urinary loss exceeds the compensatory synthetic capacity of the liver, so serum albumin falls. The reduced plasma colloid osmotic pressure allows fluid to move into the interstitium, producing oedema, which is aggravated by secondary sodium and water retention. The hypoalbuminaemia and the resulting hepatic response also lead to hyperlipidaemia, and lipoproteins that leak through the capillary wall appear in the urine as lipiduria.


## What are the causes of nephrotic syndrome?

Nephrotic syndrome results from any disorder that damages the glomerular filtration barrier. The causes are grouped into primary glomerular diseases and systemic diseases, and their relative frequency differs sharply with age.

| Cause | Children (%) | Adults (%) |
|---|---|---|
| **Primary glomerular diseases** | ≈95 | ≈60 |
| Minimal change disease | 75 | 8 |
| Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis | 10 | 35 |
| Membranous nephropathy | 3 | 30 |
| Membranoproliferative GN / dense deposit disease | 10 | 10 |
| Other proliferative GN (focal, pure mesangial, IgA nephropathy) | 2 | 17 |
| **Systemic diseases** | ≈5 | ≈40 |

The systemic causes include diabetes mellitus, amyloidosis and systemic lupus erythematosus, which are the three commonest; drugs (NSAIDs, penicillamine, gold, captopril, heroin); infections (malaria, syphilis, hepatitis B and C, HIV); malignant disease (carcinoma, lymphoma); and miscellaneous conditions such as bee-sting allergy and hereditary nephritis. Minimal change disease is therefore the leading cause in children, membranous nephropathy in older adults, and FSGS can occur at any age. In adults a secondary cause must always be excluded before a lesion is labelled primary.


## Write a short note on nephrotic syndrome.

**Definition.** Nephrotic syndrome is a clinical syndrome produced by increased permeability of the glomerular capillary wall to plasma proteins, characterised by massive proteinuria (≥3.5 g/day), hypoalbuminaemia (<3 g/dL), generalised oedema, and hyperlipidaemia with lipiduria.

**Causes.** In children it is almost always due to a primary glomerular lesion, chiefly minimal change disease (about 75%) and FSGS. In adults membranous nephropathy and FSGS predominate, and about 40% of cases are secondary to systemic disease — most often diabetes, amyloidosis and systemic lupus erythematosus — or to drugs, infections and malignancy.

**Pathophysiology.** Injury to the endothelium, basement membrane or podocytes (or loss of the negative charge of the basement membrane) allows albumin to leak across the filter. The proteinuria is called highly selective when it consists mainly of low-molecular-weight proteins such as albumin and transferrin, as in minimal change disease, and poorly selective when higher-molecular-weight globulins are also lost, as in membranous nephropathy and FSGS. Heavy proteinuria depletes serum albumin faster than the liver can replace it, and increased renal catabolism of filtered albumin contributes. The low plasma oncotic pressure causes generalised oedema; hypovolaemia then stimulates renin and aldosterone secretion and the sympathetic nervous system, while natriuretic peptide secretion falls, so sodium and water retention further aggravates the oedema. Hyperlipidaemia results from increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis, abnormal transport of circulating lipid particles and decreased lipid catabolism; lipoproteins also leak into the urine.

**Clinical features.** The oedema is soft and pitting, most marked in the periorbital tissues and dependent parts, and in severe cases is accompanied by pleural effusion and ascites. Blood pressure and renal function are often normal initially, particularly in minimal change disease.

**Complications.** Loss of immunoglobulins makes patients vulnerable to infection, especially staphylococcal and pneumococcal. Loss of endogenous anticoagulants such as antithrombin III in the urine produces a hypercoagulable state with thrombotic and thromboembolic complications; renal vein thrombosis, once thought to be a cause of nephrotic syndrome, is usually a consequence of it, especially in membranous nephropathy. Other complications include accelerated atherosclerosis from persistent hyperlipidaemia, protein malnutrition, and progression to chronic kidney disease in FSGS and some other lesions.

**Investigation and outcome.** Diagnosis rests on demonstrating the urinary and biochemical abnormalities, excluding secondary causes, and renal biopsy where indicated. Minimal change disease responds dramatically to corticosteroids; membranous nephropathy and FSGS respond poorly and may progress to end-stage kidney disease.


## What are the urinary/biochemical findings of nephrotic syndrome?

**Urinary findings**

- **Proteinuria** of 3.5 g or more per 24 hours (3+ to 4+ on dipstick); the urine protein–creatinine ratio is correspondingly high. The protein is predominantly albumin; the proteinuria is selective in minimal change disease and nonselective in membranous nephropathy and FSGS.
- **Lipiduria**: free fat globules and **oval fat bodies** (renal tubular cells laden with reabsorbed lipoprotein), which show a characteristic "Maltese cross" birefringence under polarised light; fatty casts and waxy casts may be present.
- Hyaline and granular casts are common. Red cells and red cell casts are characteristically absent or few in pure nephrotic syndrome; their presence suggests a mixed nephritic–nephrotic lesion such as membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.
- The urine is frothy and has a high specific gravity.

**Biochemical (blood) findings**

- **Hypoalbuminaemia** (serum albumin below 3 g/dL) with reduced total protein and a reversed albumin–globulin ratio. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a low albumin and gamma-globulin fraction with a relative rise in the α₂ and β fractions, because large molecules such as α₂-macroglobulin are retained.
- **Hyperlipidaemia**: raised total cholesterol, triglycerides, LDL, VLDL and lipoprotein(a), with HDL reduced in some patients.
- Low total serum calcium, secondary to hypoalbuminaemia (ionised calcium is usually normal), and a raised ESR and fibrinogen.
- Serum urea and creatinine are normal in minimal change disease and may be raised in FSGS, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis and advanced disease.
- Serum complement is normal in the primary nephrotic lesions (minimal change disease, membranous nephropathy, FSGS) but may be low in membranoproliferative GN, C3 glomerulopathy and lupus nephritis.


## How will you investigate/diagnose a case of nephrotic syndrome?

The diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome is established clinically and biochemically, after which the cause is sought.

**1. Clinical assessment.** History of oedema (periorbital, then generalised), frothy urine and reduced urine output; enquiry about diabetes, drugs, infections, malignancy and systemic lupus erythematosus; examination for oedema, ascites, effusions and blood pressure.

**2. Confirmation of the syndrome.**

- Urine: dipstick protein, 24-hour urinary protein (≥3.5 g/day) or spot urine protein–creatinine ratio, urine microscopy for oval fat bodies, fatty casts and red cells.
- Blood: serum albumin and total protein, lipid profile, serum urea, creatinine and electrolytes, and a complete blood count and ESR.

**3. Search for the cause.** Fasting blood glucose or HbA1c; serum complement (C3, C4); antinuclear antibody and anti-dsDNA; HBsAg, anti-HCV, HIV and syphilis serology; serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation (myeloma, amyloidosis); anti-PLA₂R antibody in suspected membranous nephropathy; and age-appropriate screening for an underlying malignancy in older adults. Ultrasonography assesses kidney size and echogenicity and may reveal renal vein thrombosis.

**4. Renal biopsy.** Light microscopy, immunofluorescence and electron microscopy provide the definitive diagnosis. Biopsy is indicated in adults, in children under 1 year or over about 10–12 years, in children with haematuria, hypertension, renal impairment or low complement, and in steroid-resistant or frequently relapsing disease. A child aged 2 to 6 years with typical selective proteinuria, normal complement and no nephritic features is usually given an empirical steroid trial, because minimal change disease is by far the most likely lesion.


## Write the laboratory investigations to differentiate AGN from nephrotic syndrome.

| Feature | Acute glomerulonephritis (nephritic) | Nephrotic syndrome |
|---|---|---|
| Urine appearance | Smoky or cola-coloured, often scanty | Frothy, usually normal colour |
| Proteinuria | Mild to moderate, usually <3.5 g/day (often <1 g/day) | Massive, ≥3.5 g/day |
| Red cells | Numerous, dysmorphic; **red cell casts** present | Absent or few; no red cell casts |
| Lipiduria | Absent | Oval fat bodies, fatty casts, lipid droplets |
| Serum albumin | Normal or slightly reduced | <3 g/dL |
| Serum lipids | Normal | Raised cholesterol and triglycerides |
| Urea and creatinine | Raised (azotaemia) | Usually normal, especially in minimal change disease |
| Serum complement (C3) | Low in acute postinfectious GN | Normal in minimal change disease, FSGS and membranous nephropathy |
| Antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer | Raised in poststreptococcal GN | Normal |
| Biopsy | Hypercellular glomeruli, leukocytes, subepithelial humps | Normal glomeruli with foot process effacement, or thickened capillary walls/segmental sclerosis |


## What is nephritic syndrome (AGN)?

Nephritic syndrome, of which acute glomerulonephritis is the classic example, is a clinical syndrome caused by inflammatory disease of the glomeruli. It is dominated by the acute onset of grossly visible or microscopic haematuria with red cell casts, a diminished glomerular filtration rate manifested by oliguria and azotaemia, mild to moderate proteinuria (usually subnephrotic), and hypertension, often with periorbital oedema.

The lesions that produce it share proliferation of intrinsic glomerular cells, usually with infiltration by neutrophils and monocytes. This inflammatory reaction injures the capillary walls, allowing red cells to pass into the urine, and narrows or obliterates the capillary lumens, so that GFR falls. The reduced GFR produces oliguria, fluid retention and azotaemia, and hypertension results from the fluid retention together with renin release from the ischaemic kidneys.

The commonest cause is acute postinfectious glomerulonephritis, typically poststreptococcal, in a child 1 to 4 weeks after a sore throat or skin infection. Other causes are rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy, proliferative lupus nephritis and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis. Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis is the form in which GFR declines within hours to days.


## Write down the pathogenesis of acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is an immune complex–mediated (type III hypersensitivity) disease that follows infection with a nephritogenic strain of group A β-haemolytic Streptococcus. The pathogenesis can be followed as a sequence of events.

**1. The infecting organism.** Only certain strains are nephritogenic; more than 90% of cases are traced to M-protein types 1, 4 and 12, which can be identified by typing of the M protein of the bacterial wall. The disease appears 1 to 4 weeks after a streptococcal pharyngitis or skin infection (impetigo), a latent period compatible with the time needed to produce antibodies and form immune complexes.

**2. The antigen.** Streptococcal pyogenic exotoxin B (SpeB), secreted by nephritogenic strains, is the principal antigen in most cases, and it has been localised to the "hump-like" subepithelial deposits characteristic of the disease.

**3. Formation and deposition of immune complexes.** At the outset, the antigens are planted from the circulation in subendothelial positions in the glomerular capillary wall, where they combine with antibody to form immune complexes in situ. Subsequently, by mechanisms not fully understood, the antigen–antibody complexes dissociate, migrate across the basement membrane and re-form on its subepithelial side, producing the subepithelial humps. Circulating immune complexes may also contribute.

**4. Complement activation and inflammation.** The deposited complexes activate complement, generating chemotactic fragments (C5a) and the membrane attack complex. Neutrophils and monocytes are recruited and release proteases, oxidants and cytokines, and the resident endothelial and mesangial cells proliferate and swell. The result is diffuse, global endocapillary hypercellularity.

**5. Functional consequences.** Obliteration of capillary lumens by proliferation, swelling and leukocytes reduces GFR, causing oliguria, azotaemia, and salt and water retention, which together with renin release produce hypertension and oedema. Damage to the capillary wall allows red cells and some protein to enter the urine, producing haematuria with red cell casts and mild proteinuria.

**Supporting evidence.** Antibody titers against streptococcal antigens (ASO, anti-DNase B) are raised in most patients; serum C3 and other complement components are low, indicating complement consumption; and immunofluorescence shows granular deposits of IgG and C3, the pattern of immune complex disease. Most children recover completely; a small minority progress to crescentic glomerulonephritis or chronic disease.


## What are the urinary findings of acute glomerulonephritis?

The urine in acute glomerulonephritis shows the following changes.

**Physical.** The volume is reduced (oliguria). The urine is smoky, tea- or cola-coloured because of altered blood (acid haematin); the specific gravity is normal or raised, and the reaction is acid.

**Chemical.**

- Proteinuria is mild to moderate, usually under 1 g/day (always below the nephrotic range in the typical case), and the dipstick is positive for blood and protein.
- Urinary sodium excretion is low because of the reduced GFR.

**Microscopic.**

- Red blood cells, many of which are **dysmorphic** (acanthocytes, cells with membrane blebs) because they have been deformed in passing through the damaged glomerular basement membrane.
- **Red cell casts**, the hallmark of glomerular bleeding, formed when red cells become trapped in a Tamm–Horsfall protein matrix in the tubules.
- Hyaline and granular casts, white cells, and renal tubular epithelial cells.
- There are no oval fat bodies or fatty casts, unlike in nephrotic syndrome.

These findings accompany a raised serum urea and creatinine, an elevated ASO titer in poststreptococcal disease, and a low serum C3.


## Mention the complications of acute glomerulonephritis.

The complications of acute glomerulonephritis result from the fall in GFR and the resulting salt and water retention, and from failure of the lesion to resolve.

**Early (acute) complications**

- Acute kidney injury with severe oliguria or anuria and uraemia.
- Hypertension and **hypertensive encephalopathy**, presenting with headache, vomiting, visual disturbance and convulsions.
- Circulatory congestion: **acute left ventricular failure** and pulmonary oedema from fluid overload.
- Hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis, which may be life threatening.
- Secondary infection.

**Late complications**

- Progression to **rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis**, which occurs in a small minority (probably under 1%) of affected children and is more frequent in adults.
- **Chronic glomerulonephritis** and chronic kidney disease, with persistent proteinuria, haematuria and hypertension, particularly in adults, in whom only about 60% of sporadic cases recover promptly.
- Persistent heavy proteinuria and a reduced GFR mark patients with an unfavourable prognosis. More than 95% of affected children recover renal function with conservative management.


## A child has oliguria, cocoa-coloured urine, periorbital puffiness after sore throat/skin infection. What is the probable diagnosis?

The probable diagnosis is **acute poststreptococcal (postinfectious) glomerulonephritis**, presenting as acute nephritic syndrome. The age of the patient, the preceding pharyngeal or skin streptococcal infection with a latent period of 1 to 4 weeks, the cola-coloured (smoky) urine from haematuria, oliguria from the fall in GFR, and periorbital puffiness from salt and water retention are characteristic. Hypertension is usually also present. The diagnosis is supported by red cell casts and dysmorphic red cells with mild proteinuria in the urine, a raised antistreptolysin O titer, and a low serum C3, and it is confirmed if necessary by biopsy, which shows diffuse endocapillary proliferation with subepithelial humps.


## Why is UTI more common in females?

Urinary tract infection is much more common in females than in males, except in infancy and in old age, for several reasons. The female urethra is short (about 4 cm), so bacteria colonising the introitus have only a short distance to travel to the bladder. The urethral opening lies close to the anus and the vagina, so it is readily colonised by coliform bacteria from the intestinal tract, which adhere to the urethral mucosa through P-fimbriae. Females lack the antibacterial properties of prostatic secretion, which protect the male urethra. Hormonal changes influence bacterial adherence to the mucosa; urethral trauma during sexual intercourse introduces organisms into the bladder. Pregnancy, with dilatation and hypotonia of the ureters, and postmenopausal oestrogen deficiency, which alters the vaginal and periurethral flora, add further risk. In males the incidence rises only in the first year of life, as a result of congenital anomalies, and again in old age, when prostatic hypertrophy and instrumentation promote infection.


## What is recurrent UTI?

Recurrent urinary tract infection is the occurrence of repeated symptomatic episodes of infection after the initial infection has apparently been eradicated, conventionally two or more episodes in six months or three or more in one year. It is of two kinds. A relapse is recurrence with the same organism within about two weeks of treatment, indicating persistence of a focus of infection in the urinary tract, such as a stone, a scarred kidney or chronic bacterial prostatitis. A reinfection is recurrence with a different organism, or with the same species after an infection-free interval, indicating fresh entry of bacteria from the periurethral flora; it is more common in females.


## Write the importance of recurrent UTI.

The importance of recurrent urinary tract infection lies in what it signifies and in what it may cause.

1. **It indicates an underlying predisposing factor** that must be sought: urinary tract obstruction (stones, prostatic hyperplasia, strictures, tumours), vesicoureteral reflux, incomplete bladder emptying, neurogenic bladder, diabetes, or an instrumented or catheterised tract. Unless the cause is corrected, the infection will continue to recur.
2. **Chronic pyelonephritis and reflux nephropathy.** Repeated episodes of acute pyelonephritis lead to coarse, irregular scarring of the kidney with calyceal deformity, especially at the poles, chiefly in children with reflux.
3. **Renal damage and its consequences**: tubular dysfunction with polyuria and nocturia, hypertension, secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis with proteinuria, and progression to chronic kidney disease and end-stage kidney disease.
4. **Stone formation.** Infection with urea-splitting organisms such as Proteus produces struvite stones, which in turn obstruct and perpetuate infection.
5. **Acute complications** such as papillary necrosis, pyonephrosis, perinephric abscess and septicaemia, and considerable morbidity from repeated symptomatic episodes.


## What is pyelonephritis?

Pyelonephritis is inflammation of the kidney caused by infection, affecting the tubules, interstitium and renal pelvis. Acute pyelonephritis is a suppurative inflammation of the kidney, usually bacterial and associated with urinary tract infection, which reaches the kidney by the ascending route from the lower urinary tract (more commonly, with vesicoureteral reflux) or by the haematogenous route. Chronic pyelonephritis is chronic tubulointerstitial inflammation and scarring that involves the calyces and pelvis, resulting from recurrent infection in the presence of predisposing factors, chiefly reflux and obstruction.


## Describe the pathogenesis of ascending infection in pyelonephritis.

Ascending infection is the commonest route by which bacteria reach the kidney. The normal bladder and bladder urine are sterile, so a series of alterations must occur.

1. **Colonisation of the distal urethra and introitus** by coliform bacteria from the intestine. The degree of adherence depends on adhesins, particularly those on the P-fimbriae of the bacteria, which bind to receptors on the urothelial cells.
2. **Entry into the bladder.** Organisms reach the bladder through the urethra, more easily in the female because of the short urethra and urethral trauma during intercourse, or through catheterisation and instrumentation.
3. **Multiplication in the bladder.** Normally the organisms are cleared by voiding and by antibacterial mechanisms. When there is outflow obstruction (benign prostatic hyperplasia, tumours, calculi) or bladder dysfunction (neurogenic bladder in diabetes or spinal cord injury), emptying is incomplete and residual urine allows the bacteria to multiply unhindered.
4. **Vesicoureteral reflux.** The normal ureteral insertion is a one-way valve. In reflux, caused most often by congenital shortness or absence of the intravesical portion of the ureter, or acquired from infection or persistent bladder atony, contaminated bladder urine is carried up the ureter to the renal pelvis, and residual urine again favours bacterial growth.
5. **Intrarenal reflux.** Infected urine is propelled through the open ducts at the papillary tips deep into the renal parenchyma. It is most common in the upper and lower poles, where the papillae are flattened or concave rather than convex.
6. **Parenchymal infection.** Bacteria enter the tubules and cause neutrophilic tubulitis and interstitial suppuration, with abscess formation. Glomeruli are relatively resistant. In the absence of vesicoureteral reflux, the infection usually stays localised in the bladder as cystitis.


## What are the complications of acute pyelonephritis?

The complications of acute pyelonephritis are:

1. **Papillary necrosis**, seen mainly in diabetics, in sickle cell disease and in those with urinary tract obstruction. It is usually bilateral; the tips or distal two-thirds of the pyramids show grey-white to yellow areas of ischaemic coagulative necrosis, and it may cause acute renal failure.
2. **Pyonephrosis**, when total or almost complete obstruction, particularly high in the urinary tract, prevents drainage, so that pus fills the renal pelvis, calyces and ureter.
3. **Perinephric abscess**, extension of the suppurative inflammation through the renal capsule into the perinephric tissue.
4. **Septicaemia and bacteraemic shock** from gram-negative organisms, particularly in the presence of unrelieved obstruction, diabetes or immunodeficiency; repeated septicaemic episodes may occur.
5. **Acute kidney injury**, especially when papillary necrosis or obstruction supervenes.
6. **Chronic pyelonephritis**, with coarse scarring, calyceal deformity, hypertension and progressive renal insufficiency, after recurrent or persistent infection; some patients later develop secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.

## List the causes of acute renal failure.

Acute kidney injury (acute renal failure) is a rapid decline in GFR over hours to days with retention of urea and creatinine and dysregulation of fluid and electrolyte balance. Its causes are classified as prerenal, intrinsic renal and postrenal.

**Prerenal (renal hypoperfusion without parenchymal damage)**

- Hypovolaemia: haemorrhage, severe diarrhoea and vomiting, burns, excessive diuresis, dehydration.
- Reduced effective circulating volume or cardiac output: shock (hypovolaemic, septic, cardiogenic), congestive heart failure, cirrhosis with hepatorenal physiology, nephrotic syndrome.
- Renal vasoconstriction or loss of autoregulation: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers, contrast agents.

**Intrinsic renal**

- Tubular: acute tubular injury (necrosis), which is by far the commonest, either ischaemic (shock, trauma, sepsis, major surgery, acute pancreatitis) or nephrotoxic (aminoglycosides such as gentamicin, radiographic contrast, heavy metals such as mercury, organic solvents, ethylene glycol), together with pigment injury from haemoglobinuria (mismatched transfusion, haemolysis) and myoglobinuria (rhabdomyolysis).
- Glomerular: acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis, lupus nephritis.
- Interstitial: acute drug-induced interstitial nephritis (penicillins, NSAIDs), acute pyelonephritis with papillary necrosis, acute uric acid nephropathy (tumour lysis), light-chain cast nephropathy.
- Vascular: thrombotic microangiopathies (HUS, TTP), malignant hypertension, vasculitis, renal artery or vein occlusion, atheroembolic disease, bilateral cortical necrosis.

**Postrenal (obstruction)**

- Bilateral ureteric obstruction, or obstruction of a single functioning kidney, by calculi, blood clots or sloughed papillae, retroperitoneal fibrosis, or tumours of the cervix, bladder or prostate.
- Bladder outlet obstruction from benign prostatic hyperplasia, urethral strictures or posterior urethral valves, and neurogenic bladder.


## A 6y girl has watery stool then cessation of micturition. What is the most likely mechanism?

The most likely mechanism is **acute tubular injury (acute tubular necrosis) of the ischaemic type**, following prerenal azotaemia from hypovolaemia. Severe watery diarrhoea causes loss of salt and water and a fall in effective circulating volume and blood pressure. Renal perfusion falls, GFR declines and urine output drops; if hypoperfusion is promptly corrected, the injury is reversible (prerenal azotaemia), but if it is prolonged and severe the tubular epithelium is damaged.

The proximal tubular cells, with their high metabolic rate and oxygen consumption, are particularly sensitive to ischaemia. Ischaemia causes loss of cell polarity as Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase redistributes to the luminal surface, so that sodium delivery to the distal tubule rises and incites afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction through tubuloglomerular feedback. Renin–angiotensin activation and endothelial injury, with increased endothelin and reduced nitric oxide and prostacyclin, add to intrarenal vasoconstriction. Injured cells slough into the lumen and form casts that obstruct the tubule, while the filtrate leaks back through the damaged epithelium into the interstitium. All of these factors lower GFR, causing oliguria and then anuria, as in this child.

In a child with diarrhoea followed by cessation of micturition, haemolytic uraemic syndrome from Shiga-like toxin–producing E. coli is an important consideration, but it usually follows bloody diarrhoea and is accompanied by microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia.

## Write down the morphology of renal cell carcinoma (short note).

Renal cell carcinomas may arise in any part of the kidney but more commonly in the poles.

**Gross appearance.** The commonest, clear cell carcinoma, is usually a solitary, unilateral, spherical mass of variable size that distorts the kidney. The cut surface is bright yellow-grey-white, the yellow colour being the result of the lipid in the tumour cells, and there are commonly large areas of grey-white necrosis and foci of haemorrhagic discoloration, sometimes with cystic change. The margins are usually sharply defined and confined within the renal capsule. As the tumour enlarges it may bulge into the calyces and pelvis and extend into the ureter. A striking characteristic is its tendency to invade the renal vein, in which it may grow as a solid column of tumour that extends into the inferior vena cava and even into the right side of the heart. Papillary carcinomas are often multifocal and bilateral, and typically haemorrhagic and cystic.

**Microscopic appearance**

- Clear cell carcinoma: nests, tubules or sheets of round or polygonal cells with abundant clear or granular cytoplasm containing glycogen and lipid, with a delicate branching vasculature. Most are well differentiated, but some show nuclear atypia, bizarre nuclei and giant cells.
- Papillary carcinoma: cuboidal or low columnar cells arranged in papillary or tubulopapillary formations with interstitial foamy histiocytes in the papillary cores, and often psammoma bodies.
- Chromophobe carcinoma: solid sheets of cells with prominent cell membranes, pale eosinophilic cytoplasm and a perinuclear halo, with the largest cells around blood vessels.
- Collecting duct carcinoma: irregular channels lined by highly atypical hobnail epithelium in a desmoplastic stroma.

Sarcomatoid change, which can occur in any type, carries a very poor prognosis.

**Spread.** Besides direct invasion of the renal vein and perinephric fat, the tumour metastasises widely and early, most often to the lungs (over 50%) and bones, then regional lymph nodes, liver, adrenal glands and brain.


## A male has haematuria, loin pain, palpable lumbar mass. What is the likely diagnosis?

The likely diagnosis is **renal cell carcinoma**. Haematuria, flank (loin) pain and a palpable renal mass constitute its classic clinical triad, although all three are present in only about 10% of cases. Haematuria is the most reliable clue, and the tumour often presents when large. Other considerations include polycystic kidney disease, hydronephrosis and Wilms tumour (in a child), but in a male adult the triad strongly suggests renal cell carcinoma.


## Same: what are the histologic types of this lesion?

The histological types of renal cell carcinoma are:

1. **Clear cell renal cell carcinoma** (70–80%), the commonest; cells with clear cytoplasm containing glycogen and lipid.
2. **Papillary renal cell carcinoma** (10–15%), with papillary or tubulopapillary growth, foamy macrophages in the cores and psammoma bodies.
3. **Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma** (about 5%), with pale eosinophilic cells with prominent membranes and a perinuclear halo.
4. **Xp11 translocation (TFE3-rearranged) carcinoma**, occurring in young patients.
5. **Collecting duct carcinoma** (1% or less), arising in the medulla, and the related medullary carcinoma of sickle cell trait.


## Same: how will you confirm it?

The tumour is confirmed by a combination of imaging and histopathology.

1. **Imaging.** Ultrasonography detects a solid renal mass and differentiates it from a simple cyst, which has a smooth outline, is avascular and gives a fluid signal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen is the principal investigation, showing an enhancing mass and delineating its extent, renal vein and caval involvement and lymph nodes; MRI helps to assess venous extension. Chest imaging, and bone scan if indicated, search for metastases.
2. **Histopathology.** The definitive diagnosis is made by microscopic examination of the tumour, usually the radical nephrectomy specimen, which establishes the histological type and grade; a needle biopsy is used in selected cases when surgery is not planned.
3. **Supporting laboratory tests.** Urine microscopy for red cells, complete blood count (anaemia or, less commonly, polycythaemia), ESR, serum calcium and liver function tests, which may reflect paraneoplastic effects or metastases.


## Classify tumours of kidney.

Tumours of the kidney are classified as follows.

**Benign neoplasms**

- Renal papillary adenoma (under 1.5 cm, cortical)
- Angiomyolipoma (vessels, smooth muscle and fat; associated with tuberous sclerosis)
- Renal oncocytoma (arising from intercalated cells of the collecting ducts)

**Malignant neoplasms**

- Renal cell carcinoma (85% of adult renal cancers): clear cell, papillary, chromophobe, TFE3-rearranged (Xp11 translocation), collecting duct and medullary carcinoma
- Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma), the commonest renal tumour of childhood
- Urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis
- Rare tumours: sarcomas, lymphoma, and metastatic tumours


## Write a short note on Wilms' tumour/nephroblastoma.

**Definition.** Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma) is the commonest primary renal tumour of childhood, arising from embryonal renal precursor cells (the metanephric blastema); most cases occur between 2 and 5 years of age.

**Genetics.** Most cases are sporadic, but three groups of congenital malformation syndromes carry an increased risk. The WT1 gene on chromosome 11p13 is involved in the **WAGR syndrome** (Wilms tumour, aniridia, genital anomalies, intellectual disability) through deletion, and in the **Denys–Drash syndrome** (gonadal dysgenesis, early renal failure from diffuse mesangial sclerosis) through dominant-negative missense mutations. **Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome** (organomegaly, macroglossia, hemihypertrophy) is associated with abnormal imprinting of the 11p15.5 locus and overexpression of IGF2. Mutations of CTNNB1 (β-catenin) and WTX are found in some sporadic tumours. Precursor lesions called nephrogenic rests are frequently found in the adjacent kidney.

**Gross appearance.** A large, solitary, well-circumscribed tumour with a pushing margin, sharply demarcated from the compressed renal tissue; the cut surface is soft, homogeneous and tan to gray, sometimes with cysts, haemorrhage and necrosis. It may extend into the renal vein.

**Microscopic appearance.** The classic tumour is triphasic, containing varying amounts of: (1) **blastemal** cells, small, round and densely packed with scanty cytoplasm and high mitotic activity; (2) **epithelial** differentiation, in the form of abortive tubules and glomeruli; and (3) **stromal** cells, fibroblastic or myxoid, occasionally with skeletal muscle. **Anaplasia**, associated with TP53 mutation, identifies a subset of tumours with a worse prognosis.

**Clinical features.** The commonest presentation is a large, palpable abdominal mass, often noticed by a parent, with abdominal pain, haematuria, fever and hypertension (from renin production); metastasis is most often to the lungs.

**Prognosis.** With nephrectomy, combination chemotherapy and, when indicated, radiotherapy, over 90% of children with the favourable histology are cured; anaplastic tumours respond less well.

## Write a short note on haematuria.

**Definition.** Haematuria is the presence of an abnormal number of red blood cells in the urine. It may be macroscopic (gross), when the urine is visibly coloured, or microscopic, when red cells are found only on dipstick testing or microscopy of the sediment (conventionally three or more red cells per high-power field).

**Classification.** By the timing of bleeding in the urinary stream, haematuria is initial (urethral or prostatic origin), terminal (bladder neck or prostate) or total (bladder, ureter or kidney). By the site of origin it is glomerular, when the red cells pass through damaged glomerular capillaries, or non-glomerular (urological), when bleeding arises from the tubules, the renal pelvis or the lower urinary tract.

**Causes.**

- Glomerular: acute glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy, Alport syndrome, thin basement membrane disease, lupus nephritis.
- Renal, non-glomerular: pyelonephritis, renal calculi, tumours (renal cell carcinoma, Wilms tumour), polycystic kidney disease, tuberculosis, papillary necrosis, trauma, infarction.
- Lower urinary tract: ureteric and bladder stones, cystitis, bladder carcinoma, prostatic hyperplasia and carcinoma, urethritis, schistosomiasis.
- Systemic: bleeding disorders and anticoagulants, sickle cell disease and trait, strenuous exercise.

**Distinguishing glomerular from non-glomerular bleeding.** Glomerular haematuria is characterised by **dysmorphic red cells** (acanthocytes), **red cell casts**, and accompanying proteinuria; the urine is brown, smoky or cola-coloured. Non-glomerular haematuria shows normal-shaped (isomorphic) red cells, the urine is bright red, clots may be present, and there are no red cell casts.

**Investigation.** Urine microscopy and dipstick, urine culture, urine cytology for malignant cells, serum creatinine, a coagulation profile, ultrasonography and CT or intravenous urography of the urinary tract, and cystoscopy, with renal biopsy for suspected glomerular disease.

**Significance.** Painless haematuria is the commonest presentation of bladder cancer and an important clue to renal cell carcinoma; its causes range from trivial to life threatening.


## Enumerate the important causes of haematuria.

The important causes of haematuria are:

**A. Renal**

1. Glomerular: acute poststreptococcal and other glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy, rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, lupus nephritis, Alport syndrome and thin basement membrane disease, Goodpasture syndrome
2. Tubulointerstitial and infective: acute pyelonephritis, tuberculosis of the kidney, acute interstitial nephritis, papillary necrosis
3. Neoplastic: renal cell carcinoma, Wilms tumour, urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis, angiomyolipoma
4. Cystic and vascular: polycystic kidney disease, medullary sponge kidney, renal infarction, renal vein thrombosis, arteriovenous malformation
5. Calculi and trauma

**B. Ureter, bladder, prostate and urethra**

1. Ureteric and bladder calculi
2. Cystitis (bacterial, tuberculous, schistosomal, radiation- or drug-induced)
3. Bladder tumours
4. Benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostate cancer, prostatitis
5. Urethritis, urethral stricture and trauma, catheterisation

**C. Systemic and miscellaneous**
Bleeding diatheses (thrombocytopenia, haemophilia), anticoagulant therapy, sickle cell disease and trait, infective endocarditis (emboli), malignant hypertension, and strenuous exercise.


## Write a short note on microscopic haematuria.

Microscopic haematuria is the presence of red blood cells in the urine in excess of normal that can be detected only by dipstick or by microscopic examination of the urinary sediment, the urine appearing normal to the naked eye. It is conventionally defined as three or more red cells per high-power field, ideally confirmed on repeated, properly collected specimens, since transient haematuria may follow exercise, menstruation, fever or trauma.

The first step is to determine its source. Dysmorphic red cells, red cell casts and accompanying proteinuria indicate a glomerular origin; uniformly shaped red cells without casts indicate bleeding from the urinary tract. Glomerular causes include IgA nephropathy, thin basement membrane disease, Alport syndrome and mild or resolving glomerulonephritis, which typically present as isolated urinary abnormalities. Non-glomerular causes include calculi, infection, tumours, polycystic disease, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and sickle cell trait.

The evaluation comprises urine microscopy, culture and cytology, serum creatinine, assessment of proteinuria, ultrasonography and further imaging, cystoscopy in patients at risk of urothelial malignancy, particularly older adults and smokers, and renal biopsy when a glomerular cause is suspected.
